intro: Marcelle Meyer plays the Toccata, the finale of Le Tombeau de Couperin. Repeated notes begin softly and spread across the keyboard, and the movement opens in E minor and ends in E major.

sections.label: A · Repeated notes between the hands
sections.mNote: Staccato semiquavers, played quietly, alternate between the hands.

sections.label: B · Melody above the semiquavers
sections.mNote: A melody in longer notes above the quick semiquaver accompaniment.

sections.label: Dev · Short figures between the hands
sections.mNote: The hands exchange quick figures and sustained phrases.

sections.label: Coda · Full chords and bass octaves, E major
sections.mNote: Repeated notes thicken into full chords over bass octaves.

cues.title: Opening, repeated semiquavers
cues.text: Ravel begins pianissimo, with staccato semiquavers shared between the hands. The repeated notes are short and quick. By the final pages the texture has grown to chords and wide arpeggios across most of the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Toccata, p. 24: Vif, 2/4, pp, repeated semiquavers and staccato articulation. The final pages expand to chords and wide arpeggios.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to Joseph de Marliave
cues.text: The Toccata is dedicated to the memory of Captain Joseph de Marliave, a musicologist who wrote about Beethoven’s string quartets and was killed in the First World War. His widow, the pianist Marguerite Long, gave the first performance of Ravel’s completed suite.
cues.evidence: BnF records the dedication and Long’s première: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb13917720k. Marliave’s Beethoven scholarship: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_de_Marliave. His marriage and wartime death are documented at https://interlude.hk/the-dead-are-sad-enough-ravel-le-tombeau-de-couperin/.

cues.title: First performance, Paris, 1919
cues.text: Marguerite Long gave the first performance of the complete suite at the Salle Gaveau, Paris, on 11 April 1919. The last movement bears her husband’s name. The preceding movements carry the names of other friends of Ravel’s who were lost in the war.
cues.evidence: BnF work authority gives the date, venue, pianist and all six dedications: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb13917720k. The fourth movement commemorates two brothers, Pierre and Pascal Gaudin; the others each commemorate one man.

cues.title: Sustained melody over semiquavers
cues.text: Long melodic notes are held over continuing semiquavers. Ravel marks passages soutenu, sustained, and the pianist plays the held notes and the semiquavers with different touches at the same time.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Toccata, middle pages; Piano Practical Editions, bars 130–170, including p soutenu at bar 166. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/48/IMSLP560971-PMLP4975-Le_Tombeau_de_Couperin.pdf
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Final page in E major
cues.text: The final page moves to E major, with a signature of four sharps and a fortississimo flourish. The repeated notes are now full chords, doubled by low octaves. Ravel ends the suite on a single chord.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Toccata, p. 32; Piano Practical Editions, bars 240–247, p. 52: E-major signature, fff and final E-major chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Sustained melody over semiquavers
transitions.from: A · Repeated notes between the hands
transitions.how: The piano continues its semiquavers, and a longer melodic line enters above them. Sustained notes and slurs mark the right-hand melody for a legato, singing touch, and the accompanying semiquavers keep the light touch of the opening. Ravel keeps the 2/4 metre through the change (Durand piano score, 1918, pp. 27–29).
transitions.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Toccata, pp. 27–29: sustained melody above active accompaniment in 2/4. The existing section boundary places the passage.

transitions.title: Chords and bass in the final crescendo
transitions.from: Dev · Short figures between the hands
transitions.to: Coda · Full chords and bass octaves, E major
transitions.how: The piano’s repeated notes widen into chords, and the bass line becomes heavier beneath them. A crescendo runs through this final section to the close in E major, with four sharps, at bar 240. The semiquaver motion continues in the hands through the broadest chordal passages.
transitions.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Toccata, pp. 30–32; Piano Practical Editions, closing pages, culminating in E major at bar 240.

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
